description_full: Danaos Corporation, through its subsidiaries, owns and operates containerships and drybulk vessels in Australia, Europe, and the United States. It operates in two segments, Container Vessels and Drybulk Vessels. The company provides seaborne transportation services by operating vessels in the containership and drybulk sectors of the shipping industry. As of December 31, 2025, it had a fleet of 75 containerships aggregating 477,230 TEUs; 27 container vessels under construction containerships aggregating 173,314 TEUs; 10 Capesize bulk carriers aggregating 1,755,000 DWT; and 2 dry bulk vessels under construction aggregating 422,000 DWT. The company was formerly known as Danaos Holdings Limited and changed its name to Danaos Corporation in October 2005. Danaos Corporation was founded in 1963 and is based in Piraeus, Greece.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 4 people. Revenue per employee of $260.6M ranks in the top quartile among Industrials peers, improving at 6%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Stock-based compensation of $4.2M per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: Danaos Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $2.7B market cap on $1.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 7% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 15× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 55% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 4.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 48% operating margin runs 39pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 4.35x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+7.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 84% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 14% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 24% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market.
About $21.1M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.6x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 71% in the 2020 crash, 50% in the 2022 bear market and 89% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 61% below its blended-model fair value of $378, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 27%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 5.0 vs 23.3 and EV/EBITDA 4.0 vs 13.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 189% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an EBIT/EV of 18.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $164 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 7.4%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.06).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.30x.
ROE of 13% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 12pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 1.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $2.4M (0% of market cap).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.6% over 3 years, 17.7% over 5 years and 6.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 18%).
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (4.5% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 54.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 22%.
It returns 5.2% a year to shareholders (2.8% in buybacks and 2.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 19.6% of the float, 9.4 days to cover.
people: With about 4 employees, each generates about $260.6M of revenue, 709.5x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 5.9% a year.
